notes: Protected witness unit judicial review appeal; full merits judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Protected witness removal and legitimate expectation
key_facts: Bloggs 61, a convicted drug conspirator who assisted police, was placed in a protected witness unit after giving a witness statement.
When the CPS declined to use him as a witness, the Prison Service decided to return him to mainstream prison conditions with a cover story.
He claimed police handlers had promised lifetime protected witness status and challenged the removal by judicial review.
Ouseley J dismissed the claim and the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on legitimate expectation, Article 2 and abuse of power grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a judicial review claim against the Secretary of State for the Home Department.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Prison Service's decision to remove the appellant from the protected witness unit was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Police officers had neither actual nor ostensible authority to bind the Prison Service to maintain protected witness status for a whole sentence, so alleged assurances could not found a legitimate expectation; removal from a protected witness unit engages Article 2 only if there is a real risk to life, assessed with anxious scrutiny but with deference to the Prison Service's specialist judgment on protective regimes.
legal_issues: Whether police representations could give a legitimate expectation against the Prison Service
Whether removal from a protected witness unit breached Article 2
Whether the Prison Service acted unfairly or abusively in resiling from alleged police promises

notes: Zimbabwe asylum appeal on limited UNHCR letter point.

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: A 22-year-old Zimbabwean woman claimed asylum based on membership of the minor Liberty Party and alleged past ill-treatment.
The adjudicator and Immigration Appeal Tribunal found her a credible but low-profile member unlikely to face persecution on return.
UNHCR had urged suspension of removals to Zimbabwe, but the appellant's case rested on her individual circumstances.
Buxton LJ granted permission to appeal only on the Tribunal's treatment of a June 2002 UNHCR letter.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission limited to one point from an Immigration Appeal Tribunal determination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; removal was not contrary to the Refugee Convention or ECHR obligations.
enrichment.ratio: UNHCR country guidance that opponents of the Mugabe regime face grave risks does not entitle every such asylum seeker to refugee status; each case requires an individual assessment of whether that particular claimant has a well-founded fear of persecution, and a low-profile member of a minor party who left on an official passport may fail that test.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred in its analysis of UNHCR guidance on returns to Zimbabwe
Whether suspension of removals policy is determinative of individual refugee status
Whether a Liberty Party member faced a real risk of persecution

notes: Section 288 planning challenge to inspector's dismissal of appeal.

key_facts: The claimant sought outline planning permission for residential development on land at Foredown Road/Fox Way, Portslade allocated for community facilities.
Brighton & Hove Council refused permission and an inspector dismissed the appeal, treating the site as greenfield and giving weight to a section 52 agreement and development brief.
The claimant challenged the inspector's treatment of the section 52 agreement, development plan policies, PPG3 and the finding of continuing community-use interest.
Sullivan J refused the section 288 application and declined permission to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash an inspector's appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the inspector's dismissal of the planning appeal was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A section 52 agreement reached by the local planning authority as to appropriate site use is a material planning consideration whose weight is for the inspector; it cannot be treated as an absolute bar to granting permission, but refusal on plan, brief, PPG3 and greenfield grounds was adequately reasoned and not irrational.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector wrongly treated a section 52 agreement as a decisive planning objection
Whether conclusions on structure plan and local plan policies were inadequately reasoned
Whether refusal conflicted with PPG3 on a non-windfall greenfield site
Whether the inspector irrationally found continuing interest in community use

notes: Widow's bereavement allowance HRA appeal linked to Hooper.

key_facts: Section 262 ICTA granted a widow's bereavement allowance to widows but not widowers.
Mr Wilkinson, a widower, sought an equivalent allowance after the Revenue settled similar Strasbourg claims with Crossland and Fielding.
Moses J declared section 262 incompatible with the Convention but dismissed the claim for payment.
The Court of Appeal held the Revenue lacked power to grant extra-statutory concessions contradicting Parliament's intention.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a judicial review judgment, with a cross-appeal by the Inland Revenue.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; declaration of incompatibility upheld but no extra-statutory payment ordered.
enrichment.ratio: The Commissioners' care and management power under section 1 of the Taxes Management Act 1970 does not authorise extra-statutory concessions that deliberately contradict Parliament's clear intention in primary tax legislation; where section 262 obliged discriminatory treatment, section 6(2)(a) of the HRA provided a defence and declining to settle domestic claims after Strasbourg settlements was not an abuse of power.
legal_issues: Extent of Commissioners' power to make extra-statutory tax concessions
Whether section 6(2)(b) excused failure to pay widowers equivalent allowances
Whether differential treatment of Mr Wilkinson after Crossland settlements was unlawful

notes: Permission to appeal granted; substantive s30(1)(f) decision upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Business tenancy demolition ground hotel works
key_facts: Ivorygrove Ltd ran the Crichton Hotel at 34-37 Bedford Place, Bloomsbury as tenant in common with Global Grange Ltd as landlord.
Global proposed extensive refurbishment to upgrade the hotel to three or four crown standard, costing about £4.2 million over 44 weeks.
HH Judge Green QC held the works fell within section 30(1)(f) as demolition, reconstruction or substantial construction.
Ivorygrove sought permission to appeal, distinguishing the outcome in the related Marazzi case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from a county court decision on opposition to a new business tenancy under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted but appeal dismissed; the landlord established the section 30(1)(f) ground.
enrichment.ratio: Section 30(1)(f) does not require works to load-bearing structure only; whether partition removal and refurbishment qualify is a jury question of fact and degree, and on the agreed evidence a bedrock of structural works costing over £450,000, together with associated works affecting most of the interior, was a substantial work of construction.
legal_issues: Whether removal and replacement of partition walls falls within section 30(1)(f)
Whether refurbishment and decoration can be counted towards substantial construction
Whether works were substantial in cost, extent and duration
Whether structure must involve load-bearing elements

notes: Section 459 appeal; proprietary tracing remedy against pension fund.

enrichment.short_title: Unfair prejudice tracing into pension fund
key_facts: Mr Cutland, an equal shareholder and director, misappropriated over £517,000 from Tulgrove Ltd and took unauthorised remuneration including £145,000 in pension contributions.
The company was also indebted £100,000 to a pension fund whose trustees included Mr Cutland.
The judge found unfair prejudice and ordered purchase of Mr Cutland's shares but rejected a proprietary set-off against the pension fund loan.
The Court of Appeal held unauthorised pension contributions remained traceable in equity and could be set against the loan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Companies Act 1985 section 459 unfair prejudice order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; proprietary charge and set-off ordered over pension fund assets.
enrichment.ratio: Directors' pension contributions made without company authority are void rather than merely voidable; where a director breaches fiduciary duty and volunteer pension trustees receive notice of the company's claim, the company may trace the contributions and impose a charge, with set-off against a loan owed to the same fund being an appropriate remedy under section 461.
legal_issues: Whether relief against third-party pension trustees was available in section 459 proceedings
Whether unauthorised contributions passed beneficial ownership to trustees
Whether a proprietary tracing remedy and set-off should be ordered

notes: Robinson test applied to family PKK point not raised below.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum family PKK point not raised on appeal

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: Veysel Dagdelen, a Turkish Alevi, claimed asylum based on alleged PKK involvement and family persecution.
The adjudicator rejected his account of PKK militia activity and found past arrests did not show continuing interest by the authorities.
In judicial review he argued the adjudicator ignored family members' PKK connections, a point not raised in grounds to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal.
Jackson J held the point was not obvious under Robinson and dismissed the claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; refusal of leave to appeal was lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Under R v SSHD ex p Robinson, a point not raised in grounds of appeal to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal will justify judicial review only if it was obvious and had a strong prospect of success; a subsidiary family-connection argument that the adjudicator in fact considered does not meet that threshold.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator failed to consider family PKK involvement
Whether the IAT should have raised the family point of its own motion
Application of the Robinson obvious-point test

notes: Ann Summers Jobcentre advertising ban quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Ann Summers Jobcentre vacancy advertising ban
key_facts: Ann Summers Ltd, a high-street retailer of adult products, sought to advertise staff vacancies through Jobcentre Plus during a major expansion.
Jobcentre Plus refused under a long-standing policy against vacancies associated with the sex or personal services industry.
The policy cited risk of embarrassing jobseekers asked to apply or justify refusal under the jobseeker's allowance sanction regime.
Newman J held the blanket ban irrational and quashed the relevant policy category.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of Jobcentre Plus policy refusing to handle Ann Summers recruitment advertisements.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; quashing order made in respect of the policy category covering sex-related retail vacancies.
enrichment.ratio: A public employment service must act consistently with its statutory duty to assist employers and jobseekers; banning an employer because some jobseekers might feel embarrassment, without evidence and without less restrictive alternatives such as excluding vacancies from encouragement and sanctioning processes, is irrational and fails to balance benefit to willing jobseekers against operational concerns.
legal_issues: Whether refusal to accept Ann Summers advertisements was rational
Whether reliance on jobseeker's allowance sanctioning was misplaced
Whether a blanket ban was a disproportionate response
Whether inconsistent treatment arose from the policy

enrichment.short_title: Mortgage possession appeal adjourned for representation
key_facts: Mrs Hedworth appealed a possession order obtained by UCB Bank Plc in February 2002.
Repeated adjournments arose because her solicitors came off the record and replacement firms declined publicly funded rates.
The bank opposed further delay, citing negative equity and prejudice from continued occupation.
The Court of Appeal granted an expedited adjournment so she could seek new representation before the merits hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Adjournment application at the adjourned hearing of an appeal from a county court possession order.
enrichment.outcome: Adjournment granted; appeal to be listed on an expedited basis before the same constitution if possible.
enrichment.ratio: Where an litigant in person cannot fairly meet both her primary appeal grounds and complex respondent's notice points on undue influence and subrogation, and public funding has proved insufficient to secure counsel, an expedited adjournment to obtain representation may be preferable to proceeding in a split hearing that risks further delay.
legal_issues: Whether the appeal should proceed without legal representation
Prejudice to the mortgagee from further delay
Management of a split hearing on primary grounds and respondent's notice points

notes: Property venture appeal on endowment policy and Darnley Road interest.

enrichment.short_title: Joint property venture endowment policy ownership
key_facts: Mr Owen and Mr Robert Medwin bought investment properties at Sevenoaks and Gravesend as tenants in common.
A Guardian endowment policy on Mr Owen's life secured part of the mortgage for 45 High Street; premiums were debited to Mr Owen's drawings.
After Mr Owen's death his executors claimed the policy proceeds were jointly owned; the judge held Mr Owen alone was the beneficial owner.
Proceeds from sale of Mr Owen's Gravesend property were used to repay joint Lloyds borrowings; the judge apportioned interest between the parties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a deputy High Court judge's decision on beneficial interests in property ventures.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on both issues; endowment policy proceeds held for Mr Owen's estate and interest allocation upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A common intention constructive trust over an endowment policy requires objectively established shared beneficial ownership, not merely agreement that proceeds would repay a joint mortgage; formal documentation naming one grantee, premium debits to his account, and absence of detrimental reliance by the other party prevent inferring joint ownership under Rossett.
legal_issues: Whether the Guardian endowment policy was held on a common intention constructive trust
Whether Mr Robert Medwin detrimentally relied on an alleged common intention
How interest on Darnley Road sale proceeds used to repay joint debt should be borne
